control_variables: Aeration rate maintained at 1.0 vvm (or 0.5 vvm for industrial strain bioreactor)
dependent_variables: Extracellular D-xylonate concentration and production rate
Biomass production (OD600 and dry cell weight)
Intracellular concentrations of D-xylonate and xylitol
Cell vitality (percentage of metabolically active cells) and viability (colony forming units)
Enzyme kinetic parameters (kcat, Km, and kcat/Km)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The paper mentions that D-xylonic acid or its conjugate base D-xylonate has potential applications as a polyamide or hydrogel modifier (citing prior literature), but no mechanical testing, mechanical modeling, or soft robotics mechanisms are studied.

experimental_setup: Bioreactor batch/fed-batch cultivations (500 ml Multifors and 2 L Biostats CT) at controlled pH (5.5 or 3.0), 30 °C, 500 rpm agitation, and aeration
Erlenmeyer shake-flask cultures in YP or YSC medium at 250 rpm and 30 °C
HPLC analysis using a Fast Acid Analysis column coupled to an Aminex HPX-87H column with refractive index and dual-wavelength UV detection
Freeze-drying of cell pellets followed by dilute acid extraction for intracellular metabolite quantification
Recombinant protein expression and affinity purification using Strep-Tactin Superflow Plus column on ÄKTA Purifier FPLC
Spectrophotometric enzyme activity assays measuring NADH formation at 340 nm
1H NMR spectroscopy (500 MHz) for monitoring D-xylonolactone hydrolysis
Live-cell laser scanning confocal microscopy (Leica TCS SP5) with ratiometric pHluorin probe for cytosolic pH measurement
Methylene blue staining for cell vitality and colony forming unit (CFU) counting on YPD for viability
future_work: Optimisation of production conditions and provision of higher D-xylose concentrations to achieve higher titres
Transcriptome and/or metabolome analysis of the industrial D-xylonic acid producing S. cerevisiae strain to identify pathways involved in adaptation and cell death regulation
Addressing export mechanisms, cellular maintenance energy, and preservation of cell viability for industrial production
Supplying additional energy sources (such as D-glucose or ethanol) to improve production under low pH conditions
independent_variables: Expressed xylose dehydrogenase gene (C. crescentus xylB vs. pig liver SUS2DD vs. T. reesei xyd1 vs. empty vector control)
Co-expression of C. crescentus lactonase gene xylC
Deletion of host aldose reductase gene GRE3
Host strain background (laboratory CEN.PK vs. industrial B67002)
Substrate type and concentration for enzyme kinetic analysis
limitations_inferred: The study is exclusively focused on microbial metabolic engineering and bioprocess kinetics; it provides no data, modeling, or physical experiments on mechanical mechanics, continuum mechanisms, or soft robotics.
Performance on unsupplemented crude lignocellulosic hydrolysates was not directly evaluated in bioreactor cultivations in this study.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The D-xylonate production rate in the engineered industrial yeast strain (0.44 g l^-1 h^-1) remains roughly 4-fold lower than rates reported for some bacteria (1.7 g l^-1 h^-1), which is insufficient for industrial processes.
At low pH (pH 3.0), production of D-xylonic acid, xylitol, and biomass was reduced compared to pH 5.5, and cell vitality/viability decreased substantially.
Intracellular accumulation of D-xylonate and cytosolic acidification caused severe loss of cell vitality and viability.
Spontaneous hydrolysis of D-xylonolactone is relatively slow, and in the xylB xylC co-expressing strain at pH 5.5, production ceased after 50 h despite available D-xylose.
main_results: Expression of NAD+-dependent XylB from C. crescentus in S. cerevisiae CEN.PK produced 17 ± 2 g D-xylonate l^-1 at 0.23 ± 0.02 g l^-1 h^-1 from 23 g D-xylose l^-1, an approximately 10-fold higher production rate than strains expressing NADP+-dependent enzymes.
The industrial strain B67002 expressing two copies of xylB produced 43 ± 1 g D-xylonate l^-1 from 49 g D-xylose l^-1 with an initial production rate of 0.44 g l^-1 h^-1.
Deletion of the GRE3 gene reduced byproduct xylitol accumulation to 0.5 g l^-1 (an 80% reduction) without compromising D-xylonate production rate.

Purified XylB enzyme was strictly NAD+-dependent with high specificity for D-xylose over L-arabinose (kcat/Km 400-600 fold higher) and exhibited an alkaline pH optimum (pH 9) while remaining functional at neutral and acidic pH.

Co-expression of lactonase XylC enhanced initial extracellular D-xylonate accumulation at pH 5.5 and improved production at pH 3.0 (6.7 ± 1.1 g l^-1 vs 5.5 ± 0.9 g l^-1), though it resulted in earlier production arrest at pH 5.5 and increased loss of cell viability.
D-xylonate production resulted in marked intracellular accumulation (40-170 mg g^-1 dry biomass), decreased cytosolic pH (from 7.5 to 7.2), and significant decreases in cell vitality and viability.
performance_metrics: Yield of D-xylonate on consumed D-xylose (g g^-1)
Xylitol titre (g l^-1) and yield (g g^-1)
Enzyme kinetic parameters: Km (mM), kcat (min^-1), and kcat/Km (mM^-1 min^-1)
Percentage of metabolically active cells (%) and viable colony forming units (%)
possible_gap_implications: The paper focuses on microbial bioconversion; any application of D-xylonate as a modifier for polyamides or hydrogels in soft robotics materials remains an unaddressed research gap that requires polymer synthesis, mechanical testing, and constitutive modeling.
paper.research_objective: To engineer Saccharomyces cerevisiae for efficient bioconversion of D-xylose to D-xylonate by expressing an NAD+-dependent D-xylose dehydrogenase (XylB from Caulobacter crescentus), reduce xylitol byproduct formation, assess the contribution of D-xylonolactone lactonase (XylC), demonstrate production in an industrial strain, and characterize physiological effects.
paper.research_problem: Low titre and production rate of D-xylonate in engineered yeasts due to the low activity or NADP+-dependence of previously tested D-xylose dehydrogenases, cofactor regeneration constraints, byproduct xylitol accumulation, and uncharacterized effects of lactonase activity and low pH on cell physiology.
paper.title: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for bioconversion of D-xylose to D-xylonate
